tool_diagnostics.message: apply_patch verification failed: invalid patch: The last line of the patch must be '*** End Patch'

row.note: Paul makes the omitted verb explicit: every word and deed is done in the Lord Jesus' name with thanksgiving. This is the commentary's portable opening formula applied to any act.
James corrects merchants' unqualified tomorrow plan with "if the Lord wills"; this closely parallels the commentary's extension of divine naming to future acts.
The Lord's Prayer first asks that the Father's name be hallowed before its petitions, comparable to Fatiha's unnamed act becoming praise, service, and request after the divine name.

row.basis: service and oath in God's name
row.note: The verse joins fearing and serving YHWH with swearing by his name, combining the commentary's worshiped owner, invocation, and oath functions of Allah's name.
The proclamation starts with YHWH's name and immediately names him compassionate and gracious; it is a close Biblical companion to "in the name of Allah, the Rahman, the Rahim."
Hebrew raḥum, used here for YHWH, is a Semitic cognate of the commentary's r-h-m mercy words; its setting makes mercy a named divine quality, not a free-standing sentiment.
The same name-proclamation preserves steadfast love and forgiveness yet does not clear guilt; it directly illuminates the commentary's insistence that expansive mercy does not abolish reckoning.

row.basis: meat and blood do not feed God
row.note: The psalm asks whether God eats bulls' flesh or drinks goats' blood, a pointed parallel to the commentary's claim that sacrificial meat and blood do not reach God.
The sacrifice is praise, the verbal fruit that acknowledges God's name; it closely matches the commentary's movement from animal material to piety and named praise.
The text calls doing good and sharing sacrifices pleasing to God, giving a Christian counterpart to the commentary's claim that the moral disposition of offerers, not animal flesh, reaches God.
At the authorized altar God makes his name remembered, receives offerings, and blesses; this joins the commentary's name-over-sacrifice with its claim that the name changes the ritual relation.

Israel is warned that joining a neighboring people's sacrifice and eating it draws one into their gods; this closely parallels food's altered status through a name, though the Torah narrates covenantal entanglement rather than the Qur'anic slaughter formula.
Paul says pagan sacrifices are offered to demons and not to God, making the recipient decisive for communion just as the commentary makes the name over meat decisive for its ritual status.

Genesis commands Noah and all his household into the ark because of Noah's righteousness; beside the commentary's 11:45-46, its inclusion of the household sharpens the Qur'anic denial that descent alone secures Noah's son.
God remembers Noah, every beast, and the livestock in the ark and begins to subdue the flood; this is the Biblical rescue scene beside the commentary's journey enclosed by divine mercy.
First Peter identifies the few preserved through the floodwaters, keeping the ark's protected passage central to its retelling of Noah.
The author makes the floodwater correspond to baptism; this Christian rereading changes the commentary's ark-as-mercy enclosure into a rite that saves through Christ's resurrection.
Wisdom depicts Wisdom saving the righteous man by steering him on a small piece of wood when the earth flooded, a Jewish retelling of the voyage whose movement the commentary places under God's name.
Moses comes down, sees the calf and dancing, burns with anger, and throws the tablets; the scene directly accompanies the commentary's Musa, Harun, calf, anger, and later mercy sequence.
YHWH relents from the announced disaster after Moses' intercession. It gives the Biblical side of the commentary's movement from anger at the calf toward mercy.

The psalm uses the Hebrew r-ḥ-m verb for a father's compassion to children and then YHWH's compassion to those who fear him, closely matching the commentary's Rahim as mercy directed toward particular recipients.
YHWH's goodness is said to reach all and his compassion all he has made, a close textual partner for the commentary's Rahman as overflowing mercy that encompasses everything.

Jonah invokes God's gracious, compassionate, slow-to-anger character as the reason Nineveh may be spared; it makes the scope and scandal of divine mercy concrete alongside the commentary's universal Rahman.
The verse uses Hebrew reḥem, cognate with the commentary's rahim, while God describes bearing Israel from the womb onward; it tightly joins womb imagery to sustaining divine care.

Isaiah asks whether a mother can fail to have compassion for her womb-born child, then contrasts that possibility with God's unfailing remembrance. It gives a direct Biblical analogue for mercy's maternal, protective image.
The psalm credits God with forming the speaker's inward parts and knitting him in his mother's womb, matching the commentary's claim that the one named in 1:1 forms persons in wombs.
True worship includes feeding the hungry, housing the homeless, clothing the naked, and not hiding from one's own flesh; it joins the commentary's kinship-from-one-womb and mercy-as-concrete-good.
The Samaritan is moved with compassion and immediately tends the vulnerable stranger. This gives narrative form to the commentary's claim that rahma is tenderness that entails beneficent action.
Jesus commands disciples to be merciful as their Father is merciful, an explicit movement from divine mercy to directed human practice like the commentary's Rahim.
Boaz blesses Ruth for seeking refuge beneath YHWH's wings; it offers a concrete Biblical image for the commentary's mercy as a place one enters for protection.
Jesus likens his desired gathering of Jerusalem to a hen gathering chicks under wings. The protective enclosure closely meets the commentary's womb-house image, while the refusal adds its boundary.
Approaching the divine throne yields mercy and grace for timely help, directly meeting the commentary's final pairing of Rahman with the one from whom help is sought.
The psalmist's help comes from YHWH, maker of heaven and earth; it is a concise Biblical partner for the commentary's musta'an and nasta'in connection.
YHWH declares "that is my name" and refuses his glory to another, a direct companion to the commentary's no-namesake claim and its empty rival names.
The prophet asks to whom God can be compared or likened. Its question closely meets the commentary's rhetorical question whether any being can carry God's name as an equal.
God identifies the divine name as the name to be remembered through generations; this provides a Biblical scene where divine self-naming makes invocation and memory possible.
The commentary's ilah/Allah explanation meets Hebrew elohenu, a Semitic cognate in Israel's confession that YHWH is one; the verse links cognate divine terminology to exclusive worship.

row.basis: no utterance of other gods' names
row.note: The command forbids mentioning other gods' names. It supplies a Torah counterpart to the commentary's contrast between Allah's name and names that lack divine warrant.
Paul says an idol has no real existence and that there is no God but one; it is a close Christian articulation of the commentary's empty names and single object of worship.

row.basis: Hebrew shem and Arabic ism, exalted name
row.note: Babel's builders seek to make a shem for themselves while raising a tower; Hebrew shem is cognate with Arabic ism, and the verse makes name, height, reputation, and self-exaltation a single scene.
God promises Abram a great name, a close narrative counterpart to the commentary's raising of remembrance as a divine gift rather than self-made reputation.

row.basis: God grants David a great name
row.note: God says he has made David's name great among the great ones of the earth. This supplies another named person whose elevated remembrance is bestowed rather than merely claimed.
The psalm calls YHWH's name majestic in all the earth and sets his splendor above the heavens, directly pairing exalted name with the commentary's horizon-and-sky imagery.
The moon is made for appointed times, a specific Biblical counterpart to the commentary's newly visible crescent as a temporal sign.

row.basis: sun, moon, and stars not worshiped
row.note: The Torah forbids being drawn into worshiping the celestial host. It directly sits beside the commentary's images of moon and sun rising and its warning that a celestial body can be treated as a god.
God brings animals to the human to see what he will call them, and their names establish recognition. It is a Biblical counterpart to the commentary's claim that learned names open knowledge.
One person writes "YHWH's" on his hand and takes Israel's name; name and written sign together mark membership, closely paralleling the commentary's name as an owner-identifying brand.
A mark is placed on the foreheads of those grieving Jerusalem's abominations before judgment. It makes the commentary's visible sign of allegiance an instrument of recognition and protection.
God's servants are sealed on their foreheads before destructive judgment proceeds, a Christian development of the commentary's mark that identifies whose people are protected.
The Lamb's followers bear his name and the Father's name on their foreheads; this is an especially direct Christian image of a name functioning as a public mark of whose people they are.
The beast's mark or name controls buying and selling. It offers a contrary apocalyptic development of the commentary's mark/name motif: a rival name brands allegiance and changes permitted commerce.

Jacob's agreement assigns livestock by visible color markings, so a distinguishable animal becomes identifiable as his wage. This gives a concrete Biblical parallel to the commentary's branded camel known by its owner.
False swearing by YHWH's name profanes it, closely matching the commentary's treatment of the name as both an invoked refuge and a witness in an oath.

row.basis: calling on the name in distress
row.note: The psalmist calls on YHWH's name for deliverance, giving a Biblical prayer-act to place beside the commentary's name that attaches the speaker to its owner.

row.basis: calling on Lord's name for salvation
row.note: Paul makes calling on the Lord's name the stated means of salvation, an explicit Christian use of divine-name invocation as refuge.
The annunciation says Mary's child will be called Son of God. It directly contrasts with the commentary's use of womb-rooted Rahman while denying that Rahman takes a child.

John's soteriological claim that God gives the only Son gives a central Christian form of the proposition the commentary rejects when it says the merciful divine name does not entail divine childbearing.

row.basis: single baptismal name with Father, Son, Spirit
row.note: The baptismal command places Father, Son, and Holy Spirit under the name; beside the commentary's exclusive names of Allah and Rahman and denial of childship, its different name theology is the point.

row.basis: Jesus given the name above every name
row.note: Philippians says God grants Jesus the name above every name. It is a Christian reconfiguration of exalted name that must be read beside the commentary's insistence that no one can bear or rival God's name.

The enthronement psalm calls the king God's son on the day of decree; as royal or adoptive language rather than a birth narrative, it clarifies one Jewish background whose terminology differs from the commentary's categorical denial of divine child-taking.

row.basis: justice and steadfast love over ritual display
row.note: Micah answers sacrificial excess with doing justice, loving steadfast love, and walking humbly with God. It closely parallels the commentary's movement from animal matter to the worshiper's moral posture.
James says judgment without mercy falls on one who did not show mercy, while mercy triumphs over judgment; this gives a focused Christian counterpart to the commentary's mercy and reckoning tension.

row.basis: golden calf reread as church warning
row.note: Paul quotes the calf episode to warn Corinthian believers against idolatry. This Christian reuse makes the commentary's Musa-and-calf scene an ongoing warning about rival worship.

row.basis: Creator forms life in the mother's womb
row.note: The mother tells her sons that God, not she, gave them life and ordered their elements in her womb. This Jewish text closely accompanies the commentary's divine formation and sustenance within rahim.

row.basis: letter written in a ruler's name
row.note: The royal order is written in the king's name and sealed with his signet; like the commentary's Solomon letter, sender, authority, and visible mark frame a document before its command is acted upon.
God stretches out the heavens like a curtain and spreads them as a tent. This is a specific Biblical meeting with the commentary's sky as the roof and shelter above an inhabited house.
A person plans a path, but YHWH directs the step. It is a concise Hebrew Bible analogue to the commentary's claim that an intended future act must remain tied to God's will.
Divine rain gives seed and bread by making earth sprout. It specifically meets the commentary's secondary sky-cloud-water-vegetation image, though it does not make that image a theory of names.
Jesus says the Father gives sun and rain to both righteous and unrighteous. This is a plausible Christian meeting with the commentary's rain as mercy and Rahman's wide reach.

row.basis: blessing before benefit and divine ownership
row.note: The Talmud treats benefit from the world without a blessing as misappropriating what belongs to the Holy One. It gives a Jewish rationale for the commentary's claim that naming God over food changes its relation to the eater.

row.basis: all deeds for the sake of Heaven
row.note: The maxim that all one's deeds should be for the sake of Heaven offers a Jewish ethical analogue to the commentary's ellipsis, where whatever act follows is placed under God's name.

row.basis: fetus in a protected and taught womb
row.note: The passage imagines the fetus within the womb under divine care and instruction before birth. It develops the commentary's rahim as a sustaining interior home, though through rabbinic imagination rather than the Qur'anic wordplay.

row.basis: meal thanksgiving for the holy name
row.note: The post-meal prayer thanks the holy Father for the holy name made to dwell in believers' hearts. It provides an early Christian liturgical parallel for placing food and thanksgiving under a divine name.

row.ref: Cyprian, On the Unity of the Church 6
row.note: Cyprian argues from Noah's ark that salvation is not found outside the Church. This makes an ecclesial boundary out of the commentary's ark-as-protective-mercy image.
David answers Goliath that he comes in the name of YHWH before acting in battle. It is a direct Hebrew Bible instance of a concrete, otherwise ordinary act explicitly placed under the divine name.
Peter commands the lame man to walk in the name of Jesus Christ. This supplies a New Testament instance of the commentary's bi-ism relation functioning as the means or accompaniment of an act.
The name of YHWH is a strong tower into which the righteous run and are protected. It closely joins the commentary's divine name, Noah's protective enclosure, and mercy as a place of refuge.

row.basis: putting the name upon a people
row.note: The priests put YHWH's name upon Israel and God blesses them. This makes the name an identifying, protective inscription on a community, extending the commentary's owner-mark image.
The command not to profane YHWH's holy name but to sanctify it among Israel gives a Torah counterpart to the commentary's raised name and to prayer's opening hallowing of God.

row.basis: name dwelling where offerings are brought
row.note: The sanctuary is the place YHWH chooses for his name to dwell, and Israel brings its offerings there. This directly joins named divine presence, a house, and the sacrificial animals discussed in the commentary.

The text directs Israel's slaughtered animals to be brought to YHWH as sacrifices rather than left in the open field. It is a concrete Torah companion to the commentary's meat whose ritual character depends on the one named over it.

Food is said to be sanctified through God's word and prayer. This offers a precise Christian analogue to the commentary's claim that the divine reference over food changes its status without changing its substance.

row.basis: food entering a person and defilement
row.note: Jesus says that what enters from outside cannot defile a person. Read beside the commentary's named-slaughter material, it supplies a focused alternative account of how food is or is not religiously altered.

YHWH desires steadfast love and knowledge of God rather than sacrifice. Its contrast closely supports the commentary's claim that moral God-consciousness, not animal material, is what matters in offering.

The makers of the calf name it as the god or gods who brought Israel from Egypt. This is the core Biblical scene behind the commentary's calf episode, where a manufactured object displaces the merciful Lord.

row.basis: who belongs to YHWH after the calf
row.note: Moses' call, "Who is for YHWH?", turns the calf crisis into a test of exclusive allegiance. It sharpens the commentary's link between the divine name, worship, and refusal of rival names.

Job describes the heart being enticed by the shining sun or splendid moon and the hand sent a kiss. It gives a vivid Hebrew Bible parallel to the commentary's celestial images and its warning against treating them as gods.
God places the lights in the sky for signs, appointed times, days, and years. This is a creation account counterpart to the commentary's visible crescent as a calendrical sign.

row.basis: pain in carrying and giving birth
row.note: The woman's pain in childbearing gives a Biblical counterpart to the commentary's insistence that the womb that bears and nourishes also bears the cost of birth.
A nearest relative is charged to redeem a brother's land when he becomes poor. This gives legal concreteness to the commentary's move from common womb to obligations of kinship.

God's compassion is stirred while anger against Ephraim is held back. It closely accompanies the commentary's Rahman/Rahim and wrath tension, especially its calf scene in which anger turns toward mercy.
Paul says that all have been enclosed in disobedience so that God may have mercy on all. This gives a Christian formulation of mercy's widest scope while retaining an account of disobedience.

row.basis: Son sent and born of a woman
row.note: Paul says God sent his Son, born of a woman. The verse pairs divine sonship with human birth and therefore stands directly beside the commentary's womb-rooted mercy and rejection of divine child-taking.
The name of the God of Jacob protects the petitioner in a day of trouble. This is a separate Biblical instance of the commentary's name as a refuge rather than only an address or oath.
Jesus asks the Father to keep the disciples in the Father's name. It gives a specifically Christian development of the commentary's idea that entry under the divine name is a sphere of preservation.

row.basis: teaching as rain that makes growth
row.note: Moses compares his teaching to rain and dew falling on grass and vegetation. It meets the commentary's secondary cloud-water-growth image and its association of divine instruction with life-giving nurture.

row.basis: voyage brought to a desired haven
row.note: After the storm is quieted, God brings sailors to their desired haven. This is a concrete Biblical meeting with the commentary's concern for a ship's movement and its safe coming to rest.

row.basis: sign on hand, memorial, and speech
row.note: The exodus observance is to be a sign on the hand and a memorial before the eyes so that YHWH's instruction is in the mouth. It brings together visible mark, remembrance, and spoken devotion in a way that complements the commentary's name-as-sign.

row.basis: mercy attributes recited as a prayer order
row.note: The Talmud portrays God showing Moses the order for invoking the mercy attributes when Israel sins. This makes the Exodus mercy-name formula a repeated liturgical opening, a close Jewish interpretive companion to the recited Fatiha.

row.basis: mercy toward creatures and mercy from heaven
row.note: The maxim that one who has mercy on creatures receives mercy from Heaven turns divine compassion into a directed human ethic, parallel to the commentary's Rahim as mercy reaching particular vulnerable beings.

row.basis: witnessed appearance of the new moon
row.note: The mishnah's procedure for father-and-son witnesses who saw the new moon makes communal testimony depend on the newly visible lunar form. It is a Jewish legal setting for the commentary's rising crescent becoming a recognized sign.
